The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 Clause 8.1.3 (change ends in the third game when a side first scores 11) is the standard-game rule and does not apply to this format; the format's only mid-game change is in the fifth game at 6 points (8.1.5), which is outside the question. question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' while you are playing your shot. itto-5.9.1.4 directly covers this: a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. laws-13.4.5 states that if, in play, a player deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting, it is a fault. laws-7.3 gives the consequence: the side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault and adds a point. laws-15.3 confirms the shuttle is not in play once a fault occurs. All parts of the question are answered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout is a fault against your opponent. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.9.1.4, state: "A player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)". Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 13.4.5, it is a fault "if, in play, a player: deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures". Because your opponent committed a fault, Law 7.3 provides: "The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score. A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’..." — so you win the rally and add a point to your score. Law 15.3 also confirms that once "a ‘fault’ ... has occurred" the shuttle is not in play.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) when a rally is replayed — answered by Law 14.3 (laws-14.3) and the definition of calling a let in Law 14.1 (laws-14.1); (2) every situation that counts as a let — answered by Law 14.2 (laws-14.2) and its sub-clauses 14.2.1 through 14.2.7, with 14.2.3 expanded by 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2. All parts are covered by the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, so nothing is missing and no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed when a 'let' occurs: per Law 14.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, "When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again." A 'let' is called to halt play by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire (Law 14.1: "‘Let’ shall be called by the umpire, or by a player (if there is no umpire), to halt play."). Law 14.2 of the same Laws lists every situation that counts as a let: (1) "the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4)" (14.2.1); (2) "during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted" (14.2.2); (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is "caught on the net and remains suspended on its top" (14.2.3.1) or "after passing over the net is caught in the net" (14.2.3.2); (4) "during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle" (14.2.4); (5) "in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach" (14.2.5); (6) "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision" (14.2.6); and (7) "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred" (14.2.7).

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. Both are covered by the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26: itto-5.14.2 (blood-flowing injury delay), itto-3.6.1.4 (resolve well within a few minutes), itto-5.14.1 (Umpire times the delay; Referee decides who comes on court), itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court when called), itto-3.6.1.2 (quick relief such as a bandage; no time-consuming treatment except in intervals), itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court to assist, same consideration for the opposing side), and itto-3.5.3.4 (Tournament Doctor courtside). Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.3.1 also covers suspension of play. No part is missing, so refused is false.
answer.answer:
How long you can stop: for a blood-flowing injury, per the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2, "For a blood flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise." There is no fixed number of minutes; instead, per Clause 3.6.1.4, "The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned." The Umpire times the stoppage: per Clause 5.14.1, "The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury," and "No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court." The Tournament Doctor may only give quick relief: per Clause 3.6.1.2, "The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends." Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1, "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary."

Who can come on court to help: per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.14.1, "The Umpire must try to determine the severity of the problem as quickly as possible and call the Referee onto court, if necessary. The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6)." Per Clause 3.6.1.1, "When called by the Umpire in case of injury or illness, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court." Beyond them, per Clause 3.6.1.3, "The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration." The Tournament Doctor (or other medically trained personnel) is normally already available courtside: per Clause 3.5.3.4, "At all times when play is in progress and well before the first match of the day, the Tournament Doctor (or other medically trained personnel) shall be located courtside or have a direct contact to the Referee in order to assist the Referee on court in case of a player's injury or illness." Finally, per Clause 3.6.1.2, whether your partner may continue is his decision: "The decision, however, which shall be taken as fast as possible, remains with the player."

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what happens to the match when water drips onto the court mid-game, and (2) what happens to the score. Part 1 is answered by Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.3.1 (umpire may suspend play for circumstances not within the players' control), Law 16.3.2 (Referee may instruct suspension under special circumstances), and the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clauses 5.11.2, 5.11.3, 5.11.4 and 5.11.5 (suspension warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions; court temporarily not playable → suspend until suitable; call "Play is suspended" and note "S"; on resumption note duration, check sides/service courts, call "Are you ready?" then the score and "Play"). A let is also possible for the rally in progress under Law 14.2.7 (unforeseen or accidental situation) with Law 14.3 (play since last service shall not count, server serves again). Part 2 is answered by Law 16.3.3: if play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play resumes from that point. All parts have sources; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: Water dripping from the roof is a circumstance not within your or your opponent's control, so the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire considers necessary (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1: "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary."), and under special circumstances the Referee may instruct the umpire to suspend play (Law 16.3.2: "Under special circumstances the Referee may instruct the umpire to suspend play."). The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, add that play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions (clause 5.11.2: "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions."), and that if during a match the court or its immediate surroundings is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee and play shall be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play (clause 5.11.3: "If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play."). When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call "Play is suspended" and note "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (clause 5.11.4: "When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used."). When play resumes, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension, ensure you and your opponent are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (clause 5.11.5: "When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”."). Separately, if the dripping water disrupts the rally in progress, it is an unforeseen or accidental situation, so it shall be a "let" (Law 14.2.7: "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred."), and when a let occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again (Law 14.3: "When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again."). As for the score: if play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point (Law 16.3.3: "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point."), so the suspension does not change your score or your opponent's score.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when the opponent flicks sweat onto the court. ITTO 5.9.1.6 addresses this exact conduct (throwing sweat / contaminating the court) and points to Law 16.7. Law 16.6.3/16.6.4 define the underlying misconduct, Law 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3 give the umpire's three options (warning, fault if previously warned, fault for flagrant offence), ITTO 5.17.3 and 5.17.4 give the exact calls and cards, Law 16.7.2 and ITTO 5.17.5 cover reporting to the Referee and possible disqualification, and Law 7.3 gives the scoring consequence of a fault. All parts are covered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, "A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary" [itto-5.9.1.6]. Such conduct is a breach of Law 16.6 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, under which "A player shall not: behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner" [laws-16.6.3] and "be guilty of misconduct not otherwise covered by the Laws of Badminton" [laws-16.6.4]. The umpire administers that breach under Law 16.7.1 by "issuing a warning to the offending side" [laws-16.7.1.1], by "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" [laws-16.7.1.2], or by "faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach" [laws-16.7.1.3]. In practice, for a warning the umpire calls "… [name of player], warning for misconduct" while raising a yellow card [itto-5.17.3]; for a fault the umpire calls "… [name of player], fault for misconduct" while raising a red card and "must call the Referee on court and report immediately" [itto-5.17.4]. Faulting your opponent's side means your side wins the rally and adds a point, because "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault'" [laws-7.3]. After any fault, "the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match" [laws-16.7.2]; if the Referee disqualifies your opponent, the umpire shows a black card, calls "… [name of player(s)], disqualified for misconduct", and announces "Match won by …" with the scores [itto-5.17.5].

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when the line judge could not see the shuttle's landing. laws-14.2.6 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 14.2.6) directly covers this: a let if the line judge is unsighted and the umpire or IRS cannot decide. itto-2.5 (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 2.5) adds the intermediate step: the umpire makes the decision when another official is unsighted, and only if no decision can be made is a let called, unless IRS is in use. laws-14.3 (Clause 14.3) states the consequence of a let for the rally: play since the last service does not count and the last server serves again. itto-8.8 confirms the line judge's 'unsighted' signal exists. All parts of the question are covered.
answer.answer: If the line judge is unsighted, the umpire makes the decision; if neither the umpire nor the Instant Review System can make a decision, it is a 'let' — and when a 'let' occurs, play since the last service does not count and the player who served last serves again, so the rally is replayed. (The line judge signals this with the approved 'UNSIGHTED' hand signal.) question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand court-side during a match. itto-5.12.2 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2 'Coaching from Off Court') directly answers this: coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2). Laws 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) define those permitted intervals: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, and not exceeding 120 seconds between games. Together these answer the question fully; no part is missing.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2, your coach "must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)". The permitted intervals under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, are those in Law 16.2.1, "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, except Handicap matches (BWF Statutes, Section 4.1.3)", and Law 16.2.2, "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game ... in all matches". So your coach may stand court-side only during those intervals, not during play.

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: Part 1 (plastic shuttle weight range): laws-2.2.6 gives the base weight 4.74–5.50 grams; laws-2.3.3 (Non-Feathered Shuttle, i.e. synthetic/plastic) requires the same measurements and weight but allows a variation of up to 10 per cent, giving 4.266–6.05 grams by simple arithmetic. Part 2 (special shuttle for hot weather): laws-2.4 permits modifications to the specifications with the approval of the Member Association where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable, subject to no variation in general design, speed and flight; laws-2.1 requires flight characteristics generally similar to a feathered shuttle. Both parts are answered; refused is false.
answer.answer: A plastic (non-feathered, synthetic) shuttle must have the measurements and weight of a feathered shuttle — which per Law 2.2.6 is "The shuttle shall weigh from 4.74 to 5.50 grams" — but because of the difference in specific gravity of synthetic materials, "a variation of up to 10 per cent shall be acceptable" (Law 2.3.3, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26). That works out to roughly 4.27 to 6.05 grams. As for hot weather: yes, a modified shuttle can be used, but only under Law 2.4 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26): "Subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, modifications in the above specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable." In addition, whatever material the shuttle is made of, "the flight characteristics generally shall be similar to those produced by a natural feathered shuttle with a cork base covered by a thin layer of leather" (Law 2.1). So a special hot-weather shuttle is not something you can simply choose on your own; it requires your Member Association's approval and must keep the same general design, speed and flight.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card given for misconduct before 'Play' costs a point now, and (2) whether the card is recorded after the tournament. itto-5.17.10 directly answers part 1: cards given before 'Play' at the start of the match 'shall have no effect on the score of the match' but are taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2, which makes a previously warned side liable to be faulted). itto-3.7.3 answers part 2: after the tournament the Referee must send BWF (or CC) a report on yellow and red cards that may trigger further sanctions. itto-5.17.3 confirms the yellow card is the warning under Law 16.7.1.1. Both parts are covered; no part is missing.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost your opponent a point now. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.10, misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" has been called is treated as a warning, red card or disqualification, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)" — and under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1.2, the umpire faults the offending side only "if previously warned", so if your opponent commits a further offence during the match, the prior warning means he can be faulted, which awards a point to you.
